content: Bronchopneumonia was first recognized as a distinct condition by Hippocrates, with its detailed description provided by Laennec in 1819. In 1842, Rokitansky further classified pneumonia into two types: bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia. Pneumonia can be categorized based on the anatomical distribution of lung consolidation into lobar pneumonia and lobular pneumonia, the latter being synonymous with bronchopneumonia. The pathophysiology of bronchopneumonia involves inflammation of the lung parenchyma. On gross examination, it is characterized by multiple foci of consolidation, which are typically bilateral and most commonly found in the basal lobes. These lesions are usually 2-4 cm in diameter, gray-yellow in color, dry, and poorly demarcated. They are often centered around a bronchus and have a tendency to merge, particularly in children. Microscopically, bronchopneumonia is marked by inflammatory condensation centered around a bronchiole, often accompanied by acute bronchiolitis. The alveolar spaces surrounding the bronchioles are filled with neutrophils and purulent exudate, a condition referred to as leukocytic alveolitis. There is also significant congestion, and the inflammatory foci are interspersed with normal, aerated lung tissue. The most common causative agents of bronchopneumonia include pneumococcal serotypes 3, 7, 8, 10, 18, and 20. Other pathogens frequently implicated are gram-negative bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus, and certain fungi. The mechanisms leading to bronchopneumonia include micro-aspiration, hematogenous spread, spread from a contiguous infection, and macro-aspiration. Clinically, bronchopneumonia often presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, chills, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and sputum production. However, older patients may exhibit atypical presentations, such as the absence of these symptoms or altered mental status. Gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, may also occur. Bronchopneumonia must be differentiated from other conditions that present with similar clinical and radiological findings. These include lobar pneumonia, non-infectious lung diseases (e.g., hypersensitivity pneumonitis, collagen vascular diseases, asbestosis, drug toxicities, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, and neoplastic lesions), and other types of pneumonia, such as cryptogenic pneumonia. Epidemiologically, the incidence of community-acquired pneumonia ranges from approximately 5.16 to 7.06 cases per 1,000 individuals annually. Bronchopneumonia can affect individuals of all ages but is more commonly observed in elderly patients. It is also more prevalent in men than women and is more frequently seen in Black individuals compared to Caucasians. Risk factors for developing bronchopneumonia include influenza infection, alcohol abuse, hyposplenism or splenectomy, smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and immunosuppression. Factors associated with a complicated disease course include advanced age, preexisting lung conditions, immunodeficiency (e.g., AIDS), and nosocomial infections. The natural history of bronchopneumonia typically begins with the sudden onset of fever, chills, cough, and chest pain. If untreated, the condition may progress to tachypnea, systemic toxicity, and potentially lobar pneumonia. Complications of bronchopneumonia include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess, and metastatic infections such as endocarditis, septic arthritis, peritonitis, pericarditis, and meningitis. Cardiac complications may also occur. The diagnosis of bronchopneumonia is based on clinical and radiological findings. Common symptoms include fever, chills, cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Physical examination may reveal fever, tachypnea (respiratory rate >24 breaths/min), tachycardia, and chest findings such as audible crackles, decreased or bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion over areas of consolidation, tactile fremitus, and egophony. Laboratory findings are non-specific but may include leukocytosis (15,000-30,000 per mm³) with a left shift, as well as elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, indicating systemic inflammation. Imaging studies, particularly chest X-rays, are crucial for diagnosis. Bronchopneumonia typically appears as peribronchial thickening and poorly defined air-space opacities. Patchy, inhomogeneous areas of consolidation involving multiple lobes may be seen in more severe cases. When lesions become confluent, the radiographic appearance may resemble lobar pneumonia. In cases where chest X-rays are inconclusive and clinical suspicion remains high, high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) can provide greater sensitivity and accuracy. Lung ultrasound, performed by an experienced clinician, may also be used in emergency settings. Microbial analysis, including blood cultures, sputum analysis, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and urine antigen detection, can help identify causative pathogens. However, in many cases, the specific pathogen is not identified, and empiric antibiotic therapy is initiated based on clinical judgment. The cornerstone of treatment for bronchopneumonia is antibiotic therapy combined with supportive care. The choice of antibiotics depends on the likely pathogens, local resistance patterns, and the patient’s comorbidities and illness severity. For patients without significant comorbidities, macrolides such as azithromycin or clarithromycin are commonly used. In cases of macrolide-resistant pneumonia or in patients with multiple comorbidities, alternatives such as doxycycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cephalosporins (e.g., cefpodoxime, cefuroxime) may be prescribed. Treatment response is monitored through clinical improvement, serum inflammatory markers, and chest X-ray findings. Most uncomplicated cases are managed on an outpatient basis, with follow-up visits to assess clinical resolution. Follow-up chest X-rays are generally reserved for male patients over 50 years of age and smokers. Pneumococcal vaccination is particularly recommended for individuals aged 65 years and older.
